summary: Specifies the rules for deciding whether a Unicode code point, alone or in its context, may be used in an internationalized domain name. It is part of the IDNA2008 specification. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5892 defines how to classify Unicode code points for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA). The classification says whether a character is generally allowed, needs a context rule, is disallowed, or is unassigned.

subtitle: The procedure for deciding which Unicode code points can appear in IDN labels.

tldr.problem: Internationalized domain names need consistent rules for deciding which Unicode code points may appear, including characters that need special context.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5892 assigns each code point a derived property by applying an ordered set of rules to Unicode character categories and exceptions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is part of IDNA2008 and was updated by RFC 8753. Its procedure is normative; the code point table in its appendix is illustrative.

today: RFC 5892 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 8753. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What the Code Point Rules Decide
sections.content:
RFC 5892 is part of IDNA2008. It defines whether an individual Unicode code point is a candidate for use in an internationalized domain name, either by itself or subject to a contextual rule.

The classification alone does not decide whether a complete domain label is usable. Other protocol rules address how the values apply to labels and how combinations of characters are handled.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC classifies individual characters that might be used in internationalized domain names. A character's classification is only one part of deciding whether a complete label is valid.

sections.title: The Five Derived Property Values
sections.content:
Each code point receives one of five derived property values: PVALID, CONTEXTJ, CONTEXTO, DISALLOWED, or UNASSIGNED. PVALID means generally permitted; CONTEXTJ and CONTEXTO mean a contextual rule is required; DISALLOWED is not permitted; UNASSIGNED means Unicode has not designated the code point.

The two join-control characters U+200C and U+200D receive CONTEXTJ. A code point requiring context must not be used unless a rule exists and the label satisfies it.
sections.plainLanguage: The result tells a system whether a character is generally allowed, needs a context check, is disallowed, or is unassigned. A contextual character is usable only when its rule is satisfied in the label.

sections.title: How Unicode Properties Become Categories
sections.content:
The procedure first places a code point into one or more categories based on Unicode properties or explicit exceptions. The categories are LetterDigits, Unstable, IgnorableProperties, IgnorableBlocks, LDH, Exceptions, BackwardCompatible, JoinControl, OldHangulJamo, and Unassigned.

The categories can overlap. A second step applies set rules to produce the final property value. For example, LDH includes the hyphen, digits, and lowercase letters a through z.
sections.plainLanguage: The procedure first checks which character groups include a code point. It then uses those groups and exceptions to calculate one final classification.

sections.title: The Ordered Classification Procedure
sections.content:
The classification checks the categories in a fixed order. Exceptions and BackwardCompatible are checked first, followed by Unassigned, LDH, JoinControl, the disallowed categories, and LetterDigits. Anything that matches none of these rules is DISALLOWED.

The order matters because the first applicable rule determines the result. Sections 2 and 3 define the normative procedure; Appendix B lists results for Unicode 5.2 only as a non-normative illustration.
sections.plainLanguage: The system follows an ordered checklist, and the first matching rule decides the result. The formal rules define the method; the long appendix table is an example of its results.

sections.title: Rules for Characters That Need Context
sections.content:
Appendix A gives contextual rules for characters that cannot be classified safely in every label. For example, U+00B7 MIDDLE DOT is allowed only between two lowercase l characters, and U+30FB KATAKANA MIDDLE DOT requires a Hiragana, Katakana, or Han character somewhere in the label.

The rules also limit the use of join controls and prevent Arabic-Indic digits from being mixed with Extended Arabic-Indic digits. The before-and-after tests follow the character order in the label, not its visual display order.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters are allowed only when nearby or other characters meet a stated condition. These tests read the characters in the order stored in the label, even when a script displays from right to left.

sections.title: Registries and Status
sections.content:
IANA maintains a registry of derived property values for Unicode versions and a registry of approved contextual rules. Changes to the classification rules and contextual rules require IETF Review.

RFC 5892 is a Proposed Standard in the IDNA2008 document set. The batch metadata records that RFC 8753 updates it.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA maintains the official derived-value and contextual-rule registries. RFC 8753 later updated this Proposed Standard.
